title: The ideas of Israel – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: ECFR profiles Israel's Liberal Zionist camp (Golan's Democrats, Lapid's Yesh Atid, Eisenkot's Yashar!) as a secular, Atlanticist, anti-Netanyahu bloc whose programme is technocratic governance reform rather than a break with Nationalist security policy. The camp backs hawkish policies, Abraham Accords expansion and military action against Iran, and has publicly abandoned the two-state project in favour of 'separation'.

themes.theme: Composition and base of the Liberal Zionist camp

insights.claim: Israel's Liberal Zionist camp comprises three parties: the Democrats (centre-left merger of Labour and Meretz led by Yair Golan), Yesh Atid (centrist, led by Yair Lapid, running on a joint 'Beyachad' list with Nationalist Naftali Bennett) and Yashar! (centre-right, led by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot).
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: The opposition to Netanyahu is fragmented across centre-left to centre-right lists, with Lapid's alliance with Bennett signalling the anti-Netanyahu bloc is pulling rightward.

insights.claim: The Liberal Zionist base is secular Israelis (around 45% of the Jewish-Israeli public), wealthier 'Middle Israel' and Tel Aviv residents, educated Ashkenazi middle classes, and high-tech workers who make up 10% of Israel's workforce.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: The camp's electoral fate is tied to Israel's tech sector and secular middle class, making it the political voice of the economically productive core most exposed to emigration and governance risk.
insights.quote: High-tech workers (an economically privileged group making up 10% of Israel’s workforce)

themes.theme: Historical decline of the Labour tradition

insights.claim: Labour Zionists founded Israel and governed until 1977, but their socialist model has been replaced by a neoliberal one and the once-powerful Histadrut labour union is now controlled by Likud.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Loss of institutional levers such as organised labour leaves the centre-left without a mass base, structurally favouring the right.
insights.quote: the once powerful labour union, the Histadrut, is now controlled by Likud

insights.claim: Today's Liberal Zionist camp emerged in 2019 in response to Netanyahu's re-election and was consolidated by the 2023 judicial overhaul, which brought thousands of Israelis onto the streets week after week.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: The camp's identity is defined negatively by opposition to Netanyahu and the overhaul, which may limit its coherence once he exits the scene.

insights.claim: United with Nationalists Bennett and Liberman under the 'anyone but Bibi' banner, the camp promises good governance, an end to corruption, a written constitution, term limits, reversal of the judicial overhaul and a commission of enquiry into October 7th.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: A change of government would mean institutional-reform risk reversal (judicial overhaul rollback) rather than a shift in security or Palestine policy.
insights.quote: earning them the nickname “anyone but Bibi” (rak lo Bibi)
insights.locator: Together with Nationalists Bennett and Liberman

insights.claim: The camp opposes the ultra-Orthodox draft exemption and champions a 'covenant of those who serve' — a government excluding both the ultra-Orthodox and Palestinian citizens of Israel.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Excluding both Haredi and Arab parties narrows coalition arithmetic, making an anti-Netanyahu majority dependent on right-wing Nationalist partners.
insights.quote: championing a political “covenant of those who serve”
insights.locator: Together with Nationalists Bennett and Liberman

themes.theme: Security and Palestine positions converge with the right

insights.claim: Because the Nationalists cast the 'left' as anti-Jewish and anti-Zionist, Liberal Zionists have largely renounced leftism and, in the author's view, colluded in their own delegitimisation; they trim the excesses of Nationalist policies but do not fundamentally challenge them.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Investors and European diplomats should not expect a post-Netanyahu government to materially change occupation or settlement policy.
insights.quote: the Liberal Zionists have largely renounced leftism and colluded in their own delegitimisation

insights.claim: The camp rejects annexation and denounces settler violence but not the settlements themselves, distinguishing between 'status quo' settlements near the Green Line and those deep in the West Bank.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Settlement expansion near the Green Line would likely continue under a centrist government, limiting any EU-Israel thaw tied to settlements.
insights.locator: They reject annexation and denounce settler violence

insights.claim: Together with the Nationalists, the Liberal Zionists support expanding the Abraham Accords and military action against Iran, and back overwhelming military force as deterrence tempered by restraint and diplomacy.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Israel's Iran posture and Gulf normalisation drive are cross-party consensus, so Middle East risk premia should not hinge on an Israeli change of government.
insights.quote: they also support expanding the Abraham accords and military action against Iran
insights.locator: They reject annexation and denounce settler violence

insights.claim: Despite liberal overtures, the camp is largely silent on Israeli control of 5.6 million Palestinians in the occupied territories and has publicly abandoned the two-state project, promoting at most 'separation' to preserve a Jewish demographic majority.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: No mainstream Israeli political camp currently carries a two-state agenda, undermining a core plank of EU Middle East policy.
insights.quote: has, at least publicly, abandoned the two-state project

insights.claim: The non-Zionist and anti-Zionist Jewish left, represented by the joint Jewish-Palestinian list Hadash-Ta'al, has virtually no political power, winning just five seats in 2022 and generally declining to sit in coalitions.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Advocacy for full equality and ending the occupation has no realistic path into government.
insights.locator: To the left of the Liberal Zionist camp

insights.claim: The Liberal Zionist camp is broadly Atlanticist, seeking alliances with liberal Europe and bipartisan support in the US, and would be willing to advance a diplomatic settlement involving a political process and regional normalisation.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: A Liberal Zionist-led government would likely repair ties with Europe and Democrats in Washington, easing Israel's diplomatic isolation even without substantive policy change.
